questions.stem: A 35-year-old man presented with a seizure, having had well-controlled epilepsy for several years on levetiracetam. He had been diagnosed with an Escherichia coli urinary tract infection 1 week earlier for which he was started on trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole (TMP–SMX). He had also started empiric treatment of Mycobacterium abscessus with imipenem–cilastatin, cefoxitin, and amikacin 2 weeks ago.
questions.lead_in: What medication is most likely to have precipitated his new seizure activity?
questions.explanation: Imipenem–cilastatin Imipenem–cilastatin is most likely to be the cause of his seizures. Within the carbapenem drug class, imipenem–cilastatin has been reported to have the highest risk of causing seizures. The other medications listed had reported no risk or minimal risk of causing seizures.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q6

questions.stem: A 56-year-old man presented with cough and dyspnea for 3 weeks. He had a history of gastro-esophageal reflux disease and a 40 pack-year smoking history. Investigations: CXR: right upper lobe infiltrates Sputum MCS: mixed flora Sputum AFB smear negative; mycobacterial culture positive at 3 weeks with yellow colonies.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation: Mycobacterium kansasii Clinical features are compatible with M. kansasii, but other nontuberculous mycobacteria (NTMs) may also have a similar presentation. Rapid growers are expected to grow faster, usually within 7 days. So the fact that the culture took 3 weeks to show growth eliminates M. abscessus, M. fortuitum, and M. chelonae. Between the two slow growers left, M. kansasii is a photochromogen, and the colonies are yellow in color when grown in light, while MAC is nonchromogenic.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q31

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man presented with subacute onset of multiple skin lesions all over his body. He had a history of lymphoma treated with high-dose steroids and periodic rituximab. The lesions were nodular with ulceration noted in some of them. There was no fever or respiratory symptoms. The patient had multiple pets at home including a cat, a dog, and a fish tank, but his wife took care of them. Investigations: Skin biopsy of the lesion: a granulomatous reaction was seen with positive AFB staining organisms Mycobacterial cultures of the lesion biopsy: positive 5 days after inoculation
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely organism?
questions.explanation: Mycobacterium chelonae This is a case of disseminated M. chelonae infection. It is the most common rapid-growing mycobacteria to cause disseminated skin infection in immunocompromised hosts. The organism grew in 5 days after incubation indicating that this might be a rapid grower. M. chelonae is the only rapid grower in the list. While the patient did have a fish tank at home, which is a classic risk factor for M. marinum infection, he did not have direct contact with it, plus M. marinum is a slow grower that also needs special culture conditions to grow and less likely to grow in 5 days.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q33

questions.stem: A 74-year-old man presented with fever and malaise. His past medical history included severe aortic stenosis and ascending aortic aneurysm, for which he received concomitant aortic valve replacement and aortic root repair 2 years previously. The patient had well-controlled diabetes but no other comorbidities. Physical exam revealed a new murmur. Investigations: Hemoglobin 8.2 g/dL HIV Ag/Ab negative Routine blood cultures ×3 pairs negative Mycobacterial blood culture positive after 2 weeks of incubation
questions.lead_in: What organism is most likely to be responsible?
questions.explanation: Mycobacterium chimaera This is a case of M. chimaera-related endocarditis following a valve replacement surgery. High level of suspicion is needed to make the diagnosis and to send the appropriate cultures. Incubation period for symptom presentation can be as long as 5 years. Slow rate of growth and absence of underlying immunodeficiency can help you eliminate the other options.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 5 Q35

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of progressive, erythematous nodules on his hand and forearm. He fishes frequently and remembers puncturing his finger with a fishhook about 2 months ago. The puncture wound healed well initially, but then he developed an erythematous nodule at the puncture site. He later noticed two new nodules on the dorsum of his hand, proximal to the initial injury. He now has another new nodule that just developed on his forearm.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely cause of his infection?
questions.explanation: Mycobacterium marinum This patient had an aquatic inoculation injury to his hand and then developed nodular lesions with proximal sporotrichoid spread. He most likely developed infection with Mycobacterium marinum.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 6 Q33

questions.stem: A 42-year-old male cigarette smoker presents with several months of fever, night sweats, weight loss, cough, and hemoptysis. His chest radiograph showed bilateral pulmonary infiltrates with left upper lobe cavitary disease. Sputum samples were obtained for acid-fast stain and the stain was positive. An interferon-gamma release assay was obtained, and was also positive. PCR on the sputum sample was negative for detection of Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
questions.explanation: Mycobacterium kansasii Sensitivity of PCR detection of M. tuberculosis is high on smear-positive samples. Positive interferon gamma release assays have been reported in association with M. kansasii infection. M. kansasii infection can present with insidious pulmonary and constitutional symptoms and is frequently associated with hemoptysis and cavitary lung disease. Disseminated infection may also be seen in patients with HIV .
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q32

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman presented with a persistent productive cough and night sweats. Investigations: Sputum AFB stain: abundant (4+) AFBs seen; broth culture positive on day 5
questions.lead_in: What mycobacterial species can be excluded?
questions.explanation: None of the above M. abscessus and M. chelonae are rapidly-growing mycobacteria (RGM) while M. tuberculosis is a slowly-growing species (SGM). However, the classification of RGM vs. SGM is determined by the growth rate after subculture, not the growth rate in primary culture. Rapid-growers with grow within 7 days after subculture, while slow-growers require 7 or more days to grow after subculture. Growth on day 5 from primary culture does not provide any information about whether the organism is a rapid-grower or a slow-grower because the growth rate from the primary culture depends more on infectious burden.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 9 Q1

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy who recently emigrated from Mexico was brought to the doctor because of left axillary swelling. His mother said that the swelling had been gradually worsening over the last few months, but the child was otherwise feeling well and had had no fevers or discomfort related to the swelling. On examination, he was found to have a several-centimeter area of firm swelling under his left arm with some overlying ulceration.
questions.lead_in: Of the listed mycobacteria, which would be the most likely cause of his lymphadenitis?
questions.explanation: Mycobacterium tuberculosis Of the listed species of mycobacteria, M. tuberculosis would be the most likely cause of lymphadenitis. Among the atypical mycobacteria, Mycobacterium–avium complex and M. scrofulaceum are also important considerations. M. bovis can also cause lymphadenitis but is typically associated with cervical lymphadenitis and in the context of ingestion of unpasteurized dairy products.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 9 Q34

questions.question: A 24-year-old male is referred for subacute lesions appearing on his forearm. He bought an aquarium a couple of months ago and cleans it weekly.
questions.question_raw: 20. A 24 year old male is sent to your office because of subacute lesions appearing on his forearm (see picture). Guess what… he just bought an aquarium a couple of months ago and cleans it weekly.

parts.text: [image-based question: photo of subacute skin lesions on forearm] What is the most likely pathogen (genus, species)?
Name 2 other potential pathogens.
What is the single best diagnostic test/procedure you would order, and what results do you expect?

parts_raw.text: [image-based question: photo of subacute skin lesions on forearm] What is the most likely pathogen? (genus, species)
b) Name 2 other potential pathogens
c) What is the single best diagnostic test/procedure you would order and what results do you expect to find?

questions.model_answer:
a) Mycobacterium marinum ("fish tank/swimming pool granuloma").
b) (1) Sporothrix schenckii (2) Nocardia brasiliensis.
c) Skin biopsy of the lesion for histology plus mycobacterial culture, with culture incubated at 28-30 degrees C (as well as 35 degrees C). Expect granulomatous inflammation +/- acid-fast bacilli on histology and growth of a pigmented, intermediately growing mycobacterium at the lower temperature (M. marinum grows optimally at 28-30 degrees C, 7-10 days to mature growth).
d) Clarithromycin (alternatively rifampin plus ethambutol, or doxycycline/minocycline/TMP-SMX), minimum 3 months.
questions.beyond_mandell: Sporothrix and Nocardia as sporotrichoid mimics are established teaching, not detailed in this NTM chapter.

cohort_answer.text: Pathogen: Mycobacterium marinum. Other pathogens: Sporothrix schenkii, Leishmania braziliensis, Nocardia braziliensis. Diagnostic test: Biopsy for AFB and culture (others: histopathology, PCR). M. marinum prefers cooler temp, will not grow at typical 37C incubation - must culture at 30-33C, grows in 1-3 weeks, colonies cream-coloured, key feature photochromogenicity (turns yellow with light). Treatment: Clarithromycin + Ethambutol or Rifampin; Monotherapy with Clarithromycin (less severe), doxy or TMP-SMX. Treat >3-4mo, at least 4-6 weeks before inadequate response suspected.

Which option has the best outcomes, and what is the risk in giving it?

parts_raw.text: A) What is the organism (genus and species)?
B) What are 3 treatment options?
C) Which option has the best outcomes and what is the risk in giving it?

questions.model_answer:
a) Mycobacterium avium complex (M. avium / M. intracellulare) - the cause of ~80% of culture-positive NTM cervical lymphadenitis in children.
b) (1) Surgical excision without antimycobacterial therapy (the established treatment) (2) Macrolide-based therapy: clarithromycin plus ethambutol or rifabutin (for those who are not surgical candidates or with complicated/recurrent disease) (3) Watchful waiting/observation.
c) Complete surgical excision gives the best outcomes; the principal risk is facial (or other adjacent) nerve injury. (Routine incision and drainage or partial biopsy should be avoided as it causes fistula formation and chronic drainage.)
questions.beyond_mandell: The specific ~96% cure figure and facial nerve injury risk are standard pediatric-ID teaching; MAC itself is covered in Ch. 251.

cohort_answer.text:
Most common: Mycobacterium avium complex (M. avium and M. intracellulare). Less common: M. simiae, M. fortuitum, M. haemophilum, M. scrofulaceum. Only 8% are tuberculosis in children vs 95% in adults
Surgical excision (curative and diagnostic, recommended without anti-mycobacterial therapy if safe); Anti-mycobacterial therapy (macrolide + ethambutol and/or rifampin/rifabutin x3-6 months) for those not candidates for surgery; Observation (not generally recommended)
Surgical excision (96% success rate); risk is damage to the facial nerve

questions.model_answer:
a) Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) - the most frequently recognized pathogen; in Canada M. xenopi is the second most frequently isolated NTM after MAC.
b) (1) Lymphatic - cervical lymphadenitis (especially children) (2) Skin and soft tissue.
c) (1) Mycobacterium abscessus (2) Mycobacterium fortuitum (3) Mycobacterium chelonae.
d) ATS/IDSA criteria - all of: (1) Pulmonary symptoms plus nodular/cavitary opacities on CXR, or HRCT showing multifocal bronchiectasis with multiple small nodules; (2) Exclusion of other diagnoses (e.g., tuberculosis); (3) Microbiologic confirmation - two positive sputum cultures, OR one positive bronchial wash/lavage, OR a lung/transbronchial biopsy showing granulomatous inflammation or AFB with one positive respiratory culture.

questions.question: For each of the following marine-associated pathogens - Aeromonas, Burkholderia pseudomallei, Vibrio vulnificus, Streptococcus iniae, Mycobacterium marinum, and Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae - describe the water exposure, clinical syndrome, and treatment.
questions.question_raw: Bonus: Describe type of water exposure, clinical syndrome, and treatment for: Aeromonas, Burkholderia pseudomallei, Vibrio vulnificus, Streptococcus iniae, Mycobacterium marinum, Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae

parts.text: Describe the type of water exposure for each.
Describe their clinical syndrome.
Treatment for each.
Prophylactic therapy (assuming wound exposure).

parts_raw.text: Describe type of water exposure for each
Describe their clinical syndrome
Treatment for each
Prophylactic therapy (assuming wound exposure)

questions.model_answer:
a) Water exposure: Aeromonas - fresh/brackish water; Burkholderia pseudomallei - fresh water/wet soil; Vibrio vulnificus - warm salt/brackish seawater (or raw oysters); Streptococcus iniae - fresh water (tilapia/fish handling); Mycobacterium marinum - fresh or salt water (aquariums, fish); Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae - salt water (fish/shellfish handling).
b) Clinical syndrome: Aeromonas - cellulitis, myonecrosis, ecthyma gangrenosum; B. pseudomallei - melioidosis (skin abscesses/ulcers, pneumonia, sepsis, worse in cirrhotics/diabetics); V. vulnificus - rapidly progressive necrotizing cellulitis with hemorrhagic bullae, primary septicemia; S. iniae - cellulitis/bacteremia; M. marinum - indolent papules/nodules with sporotrichoid spread ('fish-tank granuloma'); E. rhusiopathiae - erysipeloid of Rosenbach (subacute cellulitis of the fingers/hand).
c) Treatment: Aeromonas - fluoroquinolone or third-gen cephalosporin +/- doxycycline; B. pseudomallei - ceftazidime or a carbapenem (meropenem) then eradication with TMP-SMX; V. vulnificus - third-gen cephalosporin + doxycycline (or fluoroquinolone) plus surgical debridement; S. iniae - penicillin/beta-lactam; M. marinum - clarithromycin plus ethambutol +/- rifampin; E. rhusiopathiae - penicillin or ampicillin.
d) Prophylaxis (wound exposure): no firm guideline; irrigate/debride, ensure tetanus prophylaxis, and consider empiric coverage for high-risk wounds (deep punctures, immunocompromised/liver disease) - e.g. a fluoroquinolone or first-gen cephalosporin, adding doxycycline for salt-water exposure to cover Vibrio and metronidazole for soil/sewage contamination.
questions.beyond_mandell: Only V. vulnificus is covered in this chapter; the other five pathogens' water exposure, syndromes, treatment and wound prophylaxis are from established knowledge/IDSA SSTI and species-specific chapters.

cohort_answer.text: Water type: Aeromonas - fresh water; Burkholderia pseudomallei - fresh water; Vibrio vulnificus - salt water; Streptococcus iniae - fresh water; Mycobacterium marinum - salt or fresh water; Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae - salt water. Clinical: Aeromonas - cellulitis/myonecrosis/rhabdo/ecthyma gangrenosum, men:women 3:1, also leech-associated; Burkholderia pseudomallei - melioidosis, intracellular GNB, skin ulcers/abscesses failing PO abx, worse in cirrhotics; Vibrio vulnificus - rapidly progressive infection, necrotizing infections, hemorrhagic bullae, linked to raw oysters/puncture wounds; Streptococcus iniae - assoc with tilapia fish farming, impetigo/cellulitis; Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae - erysipeloid of Rosenbach, subacute cellulitis of fingers/hands; Mycobacterium marinum - indolent (mean incubation 21d), papules/nodules progressing to ulceration/scar, sporotrichoid spread. Treatment: Aeromonas – Doxycycline + FQ/3rd gen Ceph; Burkholderia pseudomallei – Ceftazidime or carbapenem; Vibrio vulnificus – Doxycycline + 3rd gen ceph; Streptococcus iniae – beta-lactam; Mycobacterium marinum – Clarithromycin + Ethambutol/Rifampin; Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae – penicillin/ampicillin/cephalexin. Prophylaxis: no clear guideline; reasonable for deep puncture/laceration, wounds needing surgical repair, wounds with water exposure outside treated pools, crush injury, vascular/lymphatic compromise, hands/feet/face/genital area, near bone/joint, immunocompromised/diabetic/liver disease. Empiric: 1st gen cephalosporin OR clindamycin + fluoroquinolone; salt water add doxycycline; soil/sewage add metronidazole; wash wound, debride, tetanus prophylaxis
